suggestions.rationale: Require documented mild traumatic brain injury plus a new headache developing within the ICHD-3 temporal attribution window. For core ICHD-3 publication, headache onset should be within 7 days after injury, regaining consciousness, or discontinuation of medication that impaired the ability to sense/report headache. Persistent subtype requires duration greater than 3 months.
evidenceGaps: Neurology or headache-specialist diagnosis distinguishing migraine from other post-traumatic headache phenotypes
Headache onset chronology relative to the mild TBI, including the temporal criteria used for post-traumatic headache
Headache frequency, duration, associated migraine features, and longitudinal treatment records
Pre-injury headache or migraine history and other competing headache causes
Clinician assessment addressing whether the individual's diagnosed migraine/post-traumatic headache phenotype is attributable to the documented mTBI

suggestions.rationale: Mapping Expansion Batch ME-2 adds this relationship only as a bounded clinical proposition. Require documented mild traumatic brain injury/concussion followed by separately documented persistent post-concussive symptoms extending beyond the acute recovery period, with clinical attribution to the qualifying injury. Do not infer post-concussion syndrome from transient acute headache, dizziness, cognitive complaints, or other symptoms occurring only immediately after injury. Consider pre-existing psychiatric, sleep, neurologic, and symptom conditions that may contribute to or mimic persistent post-concussive symptoms. The cited literature supports only this constrained relationship and does not, by itself, establish an individual medical nexus.
evidenceGaps: Independent documentation of mild-tbi and post-concussion-syndrome
Chronology and phenotype compatible with the bounded source proposition
Assessment of competing etiologies, shared risk factors, and treatment effects where applicable

Resolution of the approved publication guard: Require documented mild traumatic brain injury/concussion followed by separately documented persistent post-concussive symptoms extending beyond the acute recovery period, with clinical attribution to the qualifying injury. Consider pre-existing psychiatric, sleep, neurologic, and symptom conditions that may contribute to or mimic persistent post-concussive symptoms.
